761.quote_or_event: At his succession in 1606, after his father Guru Arjan's martyrdom, Guru Hargobind is said to have worn two swords, one for temporal authority (miri) and one for spiritual authority (piri). He built up a standing Sikh army and gave the faith a military side it had not had before.
761.explanation: Sikh tradition remembers Guru Hargobind as the Guru who made an organised armed force part of the community's life, with the Akal Takht as the seat of temporal authority facing the Harmandir Sahib.
761.tie_back: The Kural ranks a complete, fearless army first among a ruler's treasures; Guru Hargobind's reform is the moment Sikhism decided that the community needed such an army to protect itself, though always beneath the authority of piri, the spiritual sword.
761._accuracy_note: A genuine Sikh turn toward valuing an army, but Sikhism never ranks the army above the Name; Gurbani (e.g. Ang 142) says armies are worthless without it, so the fit is partial.

762.quote_or_event: “He alone is known as a spiritual hero, who fights in defense of religion. He may be cut apart, piece by piece, but he never leaves the field of battle.”
762.explanation: Bhagat Kabir's salok, kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, defines the true hero as one who holds the field even while being cut down piece by piece.
762.tie_back: The Kural praises courage that stands firm even after defeat and heavy losses; Kabir's hero likewise does not leave the field however much he is cut down.
762.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maaroo, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
762._accuracy_note: A strong image of holding firm under attrition, but Kabir speaks of an individual (and largely spiritual) warrior, not of a long-established army as a body.

763.quote_or_event: At Chamkaur in December 1704, after the evacuation of Anandpur, Guru Gobind Singh, his two elder sons and about forty Sikhs held a mud fortress against a far larger Mughal-led force. The Guru's elder sons Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh died fighting there.
763.explanation: Sikh memory treats Chamkaur as the classic case of a tiny band of Khalsa holding off a vast besieging army through sheer resolve.
763.tie_back: The Kural says a host of rats roaring like the sea scatters at one breath of the cobra; Chamkaur is remembered in the same terms, with a handful of committed fighters standing against a multitude.
763.source: Wikipedia, 'Battle of Chamkaur' (paraphrase of traditional and historical accounts)
763._accuracy_note: A good thematic parallel, but Chamkaur was a costly stand rather than a rout of the enemy, figures for the Mughal force vary widely, and Wikipedia is used as a last-resort source.

764.quote_or_event: After Anandpur was abandoned, Guru Gobind Singh's two youngest sons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, were taken before Wazir Khan, governor of Sirhind, and offered rewards and an easy life if they would give up their faith. They refused and were put to death in December 1705; popular tradition says they were bricked up alive.
764.explanation: The younger Sahibzade are honoured in Sikh tradition as children who could not be bought, holding to the courage of their father and their grandfather Guru Tegh Bahadur.
764.tie_back: The Kural's true army cannot be won over by the enemy and carries a courage handed down through generations; the Sahibzade refused every bribe and showed the inherited resolve of their line.
764._accuracy_note: Matches 'cannot be won over' and 'inherited courage' well, but concerns two children rather than an army; the bricking detail is traditional, and Wikipedia is a last-resort source.

765.quote_or_event: On Baisakhi in 1699 at Anandpur, Guru Gobind Singh asked for volunteers ready to give their heads. Five came forward, and they became the Panj Pyare, the first initiates of the Khalsa, drinking amrit stirred with a double-edged sword from one bowl and all taking the name Singh.
765.explanation: The Khalsa was founded as one body of initiates, of mixed backgrounds, who had shown at the start that they would face death together.
765.tie_back: The Kural says the true army is one that stands together and faces even Death in fury; the Khalsa began with men ready to die, joined by a shared initiation into a single body.
765.source: The Conversation, 'Why Sikhs celebrate the festival of Baisakhi' (2024) (paraphrase)
765._accuracy_note: A strong fit for collective resolve before death, though the Khalsa is a religious order and not only an army; some details (the five names, whether the 'beheadings' were staged) differ between accounts.

766.quote_or_event: “If a servant, performing service, obeys the Will of his Master, his honor increases, and he receives double his wages. But if he claims to be equal to his Master, he earns his Master’s displeasure.”
766.explanation: Guru Angad's pauri in Asa di Vaar says that a servant earns honour by faithfully obeying his master's will, and loses it through arrogance.
766.tie_back: The Kural lists honour and being trusted by the king among an army's safeguards; Guru Angad ties honour to faithful service under a master's will, though he speaks of the soul serving God.
766.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, pauri 22), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
766._accuracy_note: Covers only honour and trusted service among the four qualities, and the master meant is God, not a king; a next-best match.

767.quote_or_event: During the first siege of Anandpur on 1 September 1700, the hill chiefs sent a drunken, armour-plated elephant to batter down the gate of Lohgarh Fort. Guru Gobind Singh chose Bhai Bachittar Singh to meet it; he rode out and drove his spear through the plate into its forehead, and the wounded elephant turned back into the besiegers' ranks.
767.explanation: The episode is celebrated in Sikh tradition as a single warrior meeting the head of the enemy's assault and turning it back.
767.tie_back: The Kural's true army knows how to withstand the attack and bears the brunt of the enemy's vanguard; Bachittar Singh met the very spearhead of the assault at the gate and broke it.
767.source: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, 'Bachittar Singh, Bhai (d. 1705)', citing Gurbilas Patshahi 10 (paraphrase)
767._accuracy_note: A vivid parallel for meeting the enemy's vanguard; it rests on the eighteenth-century Gurbilas account and is one warrior's act rather than a whole army's.

768.quote_or_event: Guru Gobind Singh held the first Hola Mahalla at Anandpur in February 1701, turning the spring festival of Holi into an organised procession and display of martial skill, with simulated battles near Holgarh Fort.
768.explanation: Hola Mahalla was a public show of the Khalsa's array and training, and Nihangs still lead the procession at Anandpur today.
768.tie_back: The Kural says an army can win renown by the splendour of its array alone; Hola Mahalla was exactly such a display of ordered strength.
768.source: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, 'Hola Mahalla' (paraphrase; text as reprinted by Asia Samachar, 2015)
768._accuracy_note: A good parallel for martial display, though Hola Mahalla was training and celebration rather than a substitute for fighting strength; the entry was read in a reprint, not on the encyclopaedia's own page.

769.quote_or_event: “I am so hungry, I cannot perform devotional worship. Here, Lord, take back Your mala.”
769.explanation: In this frank hymn Kabir admits that real want undermines even devotion, and asks God for simple food, a bed and a quilt so that he can serve wholeheartedly.
769.tie_back: The Kural says an army wins if it is free of want and lasting discontent; Kabir makes the same point about the devotee, whose service cannot last on an empty stomach.
769.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 656, Raag Sorath, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
769._accuracy_note: Shares the insight that want destroys morale, but concerns a devotee's needs rather than an army's pay and supply; a next-best match.

770.quote_or_event: “If a hundred moons were to rise, and a thousand suns appeared, even with such light, there would still be pitch darkness without the Guru.”
770.explanation: Guru Angad's salok says that no amount of light is any use without the Guru to guide.
770.tie_back: The Kural says an army with steadfast soldiers in plenty cannot stand without worthy leaders; Guru Angad says that a hundred moons and a thousand suns still leave darkness without the Guru.
770.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 463, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
770._accuracy_note: A close structural parallel (great numbers are useless without the leader), but the Guru is a spiritual guide, not a military commander.
